statement: Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park was excluded from the Aboriginal Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act 1976 initially because it had operated as a reserve since the 1950s; Anangu, the Pitjantjatjara Council, and the Central Land Council lobbied through the late 1970s for an amendment permitting a claim. On 26 October 1985, Governor-General Sir Ninian Stephen presented title deeds to Anangu traditional owners at a ceremony at Mutitjulu; title was immediately leased back for 99 years to the federal parks agency, establishing a joint-management structure (majority-Anangu Board of Management) still in force. A legally and geographically distinct earlier statute, the Anangu Pitjantjatjara Yankunytjatjara Land Rights Act 1981 (South Australia), covers the SA Pitjantjatjara/Yankunytjatjara/Ngaanyatjarra lands around the Musgrave Ranges, NOT Uluru-Kata Tjuta — the two should not be conflated. The Uluru-Kata Tjuta Board of Management voted unanimously in November 2017 to close the climb once visitor-climb rates fell below 20%; the permanent closure took effect 26 October 2019, deliberately set as the 34th anniversary of the handback, after Anangu had informally requested visitors not climb since at least 1985.

sources.citation: National Museum of Australia, "Handback of Uluru to the Anangu," Defining Moments.
